alignment.note: Greek and Vulgate open with the connective καί / et; the Peshitta omits the initial coordinating conjunction here, instead deferring its discourse marker to the postpositive ܕܝܢ, a stylistic Syriac preference for placing the connective after the verb.

The Greek imperfect ἐκάθητο and Latin imperfect sedebat are rendered in Syriac by the periphrastic ܝܬܒ ܗܘܐ (perfect verb + auxiliary ܗܘܐ), the standard Syriac means of expressing durative or continuous past action.

The Greek δέ ('now/but') corresponds to the Peshitta postpositive ܕܝܢ, a direct Syriac borrowing reflecting the same adversative/continuative force; the Vulgate carries no equivalent particle, having spent its connective on the opening et.
The pronominal object 'him' is fused into the Syriac form ܚܕܪܘܗܝ ('around him') as an enclitic suffix rather than a separate token.
Greek marks the clause break with καί and the Vulgate with a colon; the Peshitta has no separate token here, its conjunction being prefixed to the following verb ܘܐܡܪܘ.

Greek λέγουσιν and Vulgate dicunt are present-tense (historic present) 3rd plural; the Peshitta ܘܐܡܪܘ is a perfect ('and they said'), reflecting the common Syriac tendency to render the Greek historic present as a simple past.
The dative αὐτῷ / ܠܗ / ei ('to him'); the Vulgate appends a second colon (idx 9) introducing direct speech.
The articular ἡ μήτηρ is rendered without article in Syriac and Latin, which lack the definite article in this construction.
The possessive σου / tua is expressed in Syriac as the enclitic suffix on ܐܡܟ ('your mother').
οἱ ἀδελφοί σου / fratres tui ('your brothers') is compressed in Syriac to the single suffixed form ܘܐܚܝܟ, which carries the conjunction, noun, and possessive together.

The Greek alone (per the longer Western/Caesarean reading) includes καὶ αἱ ἀδελφαί σου ('and your sisters'); both the Peshitta and the Vulgate omit the sisters entirely, agreeing with the dominant Alexandrian text-type which lacks this clause at Mark 3:32.

Greek ζητοῦσίν and Latin quærunt are 3rd plural present; the Syriac ܒܥܝܢ is a participial/predicative form agreeing with the plural subject, expressing ongoing action ('are seeking') consistent with the Greek progressive sense.
The accusative object σε / ܠܟ / te ('you'); the Greek closes the pericope with a paragraph marker (¶).
